items.title: Why the Next AI Breakthrough May Come from Physics with Max Welling - #774
items.summary: The conventional wisdom in AI is that the next breakthrough will come from more compute, more data, and larger models. But what if the next leap comes from somewhere else? In this episode, Max Welling—co-founder and CTO of CuspAI and professor at the University of Amsterdam—argues that physics may provide some of the ideas behind the next generation of AI systems. We begin with CuspAI’s work using generative AI to design entirely new materials for semiconductors, batteries, carbon capture, and clean energy. Max explains how foundation models for chemistry, agentic workflows, simulation, and automated experimentation are dramatically accelerating the search for new materials and reshaping scientific discovery. The conversation then broadens into a deeper question. Beyond giving AI new scientific problems to solve, can physics also teach us how to build better AI? Max explores surprising connections between machine learning and thermodynamics, why waves may become a new computational primitive for neural networks, and how concepts like symmetry breaking and statistical physics could inspire AI architectures beyond today’s scaling paradigm. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/774.

Why Image Generation Needs More Than Bigger Models with Fatih Porikli - #773
items.summary: Text-to-image models have become remarkably good at producing realistic images. But realism isn’t the same as correctness. Ask for several distinct people, a specific composition, or a high-resolution image generated locally, and today’s models still struggle in surprising ways. In this episode, Fatih Porikli, Vice President of Technology at Qualcomm, joins me to discuss what remains unsolved in image generation and several approaches his team presented at CVPR to address those challenges. We explore why better training objectives can improve controllability, how separating scene planning from rendering may lead to more reliable image generation, techniques for generating 16-megapixel images efficiently on edge devices, and new methods for eliminating the visible artifacts that often appear in AI-powered image editing. Along the way, we discuss reinforcement learning for image generation, agentic image generation pipelines, on-device AI, and what the next phase of progress in generative vision systems is likely to look like. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/773

Why Models Are AI’s Next Training Dataset with Damian Borth - #772
items.summary: For more than a decade, AI has advanced by training ever-larger models on ever-larger datasets. But as high-quality training data becomes harder to find and pretraining grows increasingly expensive, researchers are looking for new ways to keep foundation models improving. In this episode, Damian Borth, professor of AI and machine learning at the University of St. Gallen, argues we’ve been overlooking an important source of knowledge: the models we’ve already trained. His group’s work on weight space learning treats trained neural networks themselves as data, learning from the distilled results of millions of GPU hours of optimization rather than starting from raw data each time. We explore what it means to build foundation models of neural networks, how knowledge can be transferred across architectures and domains, why this approach could dramatically reduce the cost of developing specialized models, and whether future AI systems may be trained on collections of existing models instead of ever-growing datasets. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/772.

items.title: How AI Learns to Smell with Alex Wiltschko - #771
items.summary: In this episode, Alex Wiltschko, founder and CEO of Osmo, joins the show to discuss his goal of giving computers a sense of smell and what it takes to build olfactory intelligence. We explore the science behind smell, from the hundreds of olfactory receptors in the human nose to the challenge of mapping the relationship between molecular structure and odor, ensuring safety regulations are met, and building foundation models for smell. Alex explains how graph neural networks and advanced embedding spaces allow AI to capture the multi-dimensional structure of scents, grouping them into perceptual neighborhoods, and creating a machine learning representation that predicts how molecules smell. We also cover how Osmo built the largest proprietary olfactory dataset from scratch to train a fleet of predictive models, and how olfactory intelligence could eventually power applications far beyond fragrance, including disease detection, emotion sensing, and consumer devices. 🗒️ Full show notes: https://twimlai.com/go/771.

it.title: Risorse per corsi di IA in Python, C# e Lean4 su GitHub
it.summary: Il repository GitHub jsboige/CoursIA raccoglie risorse didattiche e laboratori pratici per l'intelligenza artificiale, scritti in Python, C# e Lean4. Aggiornato recentemente, offre materiali mirati per lo studio di queste tecnologie.
it.why_it_matters: La disponibilità di materiali di studio multilinguaggio in Python, C# e Lean4 facilita l'apprendimento pratico dell'intelligenza artificiale su piattaforme aperte.
it.extended_analysis:
Il deposito offre materiali didattici e TPs dedicati all'intelligenza artificiale, coprendo linguaggi come Python, C# e Lean4. Sebbene le informazioni disponibili siano limitate, la combinazione di questi ambienti di programmazione e verifica formale rappresenta una risorsa utile per studenti e docenti.

Sarà importante monitorare futuri aggiornamenti del repository per verificare l'espansione dei contenuti e la struttura dei laboratori proposti.
it.context: I repository di codice aperto su GitHub sono strumenti fondamentali per la condivisione di materiali didattici e risorse pratiche nell'ambito dell'istruzione tecnologica.
key_takeaways: Raccolta di risorse didattiche e TPs per l'intelligenza artificiale.
Utilizzo dei linguaggi Python, C# e Lean4.
Repository disponibile pubblicamente su GitHub.
highlights: Contiene risorse in Python, C# e Lean4.
Aggiornato a novembre 2026.

en.title: AI Course Resources in Python, C#, and Lean4 on GitHub
en.summary: The GitHub repository jsboige/CoursIA provides educational resources and practical labs for artificial intelligence using Python, C#, and Lean4. Recently updated, it serves as a practical reference for learners and educators.
en.why_it_matters: Access to open educational materials across multiple programming languages supports structured learning and hands-on practice in artificial intelligence.
en.extended_analysis:
The repository contains course resources and practical exercises (TPs) focusing on AI across Python, C#, and Lean4. Given the description is relatively brief, further details on curriculum depth depend on inspecting the source repository directly.

Observers should watch for subsequent updates or contributions to the repository to see how the course structure and lab materials evolve over time.
en.context: Open-source repositories on platforms like GitHub serve as common hubs for distributing educational curricula and technical documentation.
key_takeaways: Educational repository for artificial intelligence courses.
Implements Python, C#, and Lean4.
Hosted publicly on GitHub.
highlights: Includes course resources and practical labs.
Features Jupyter Notebook as a primary programming language environment.

de.extended_analysis:
Das Repository enthält Kursressourcen und praktische Aufgaben (TPs) mit Schwerpunkt auf KI unter Verwendung von Python, C# und Lean4. Da die Beschreibung kurz gehalten ist, lässt sich der genaue Umfang am besten direkt im Quellcode-Repository einsehen.

Es empfiehlt sich, künftige Aktualisierungen des Repositorys zu beobachten, um die Entwicklung der Kursinhalte und Laborübungen zu verfolgen.
de.context: Open-Source-Repositories auf Plattformen wie GitHub dienen als gängige Anlaufstellen für die Bereitstellung von Bildungs- und Kursmaterialien.

Öffentlich zugänglich auf GitHub.
highlights: Beinhaltet Kursmaterialien und TPs.
